title: A crash, and recovery from the log
sub: Two transactions on three pages. T1 commits; T2 is interrupted.

frames.caption: Three pages, A, B and C, each cached in memory and stored in the data file on disk. The log on disk is empty.
T1 sets A = 5. The page changes in memory only (it is now dirty: newer than its copy on disk), and a log record is appended to the log buffer. It holds the old and new value.
T1 sets B = 7. Another record. Nothing has touched the data file.

T1 commits: append a commit record and fsync the log. That one sequential write is the moment of durability; only now is the client told "committed". The data file still says A=1, B=1, and that is fine.
T2 starts and sets C = 9. It has not committed.

Memory is tight, so the buffer manager writes dirty page C to disk early, even though T2 is unfinished. The rule that makes this safe: the log record goes to disk before the page does. That is the "write-ahead" in the name.
A background writer also flushes page A. The data file is now a mixture: one committed change (A=5), one committed change missing (B is still 1), and one uncommitted change present (C=9).
Crash. Memory is gone. The data file on its own is wrong in two ways. But the log on disk has everything needed to fix it.
Redo. Replay every logged change in order, starting from the last checkpoint. A is already 5 (harmless to repeat), B becomes 7, C stays 9. Disk now matches the moment of the crash.

Undo. T2 has no commit record, so roll it back using the old value in its record: C returns to 1, and an abort record is logged. Result: every committed write survived, and no trace of the unfinished one remains.
